{{Libertarian socialism sidebar|people}}

'''Michael Albert''' (born April 8, 1947) is an American economist, speaker, writer, and political critic. Since the late 1970s, he has published on a variety of subjects. He has set up his own media outfits, magazines, and podcasts. He is known for helping to develop the [[socioeconomic]] theory of [[participatory economics]].{{r|redpepper}}

==Biography==
Albert was born in New York City and grew up in [[New Rochelle, New York]].<ref>{{YouTube|id=ikOm-nE3l3o&t=198s|title="Michael Albert on MIT, Secret Societies, and Powerful Institutions"}}</ref> In 1965, Albert was studying [[physics]] at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]]. He objected to the US military's funding of the university. This, along with the [[civil rights movement]], led Albert to become politically active.{{r|chom|page=39|mase}} He became a member of [[Students for a Democratic Society (1960 organization)|Students for a Democratic Society]] and [[Opposition to the Vietnam War|opposed the Vietnam War]]. He was expelled from MIT, in January 1970, for disruptive behaviour,{{r|mase}}{{r|macrimson}} although he claimed the charges were 'cooked-up'.{{r|cook}}

Albert founded [[South End Press]] in 1977{{r|mase}} along with [[Lydia Sargent]] and [[Juliet Schor]],{{r|ias}} among others.

In 1987, Albert founded ''Zeta Magazine'' with Sargent.{{r|nspilger1}} The magazine focused on libertarian and anarchist socialist thought.{{r|roar}} It was renamed ''Z Magazine'' in 1989.{{r|monthly}}

In 1990–91, Albert and [[Robin Hahnel]] worked on outlining their ideas around participatory economics. They published ''Looking Forward'' and ''The Political Economy of Participatory Economics'', with the latter including an [[economic model]] of the system.{{r|jei}}{{r|lib}} Doug Brown, writing in the ''[[Journal of Economic Issues]]'' said their alternative to markets was novel, but mainly of academic interest.{{r|jei}}

By 1995, the organisation ''Z Magazine'' had branched out providing online content and media training. Along with the magazine the ventures are collectively known as ''[[Z Communications]]''.{{r|iops2}}

In 2003, ''Parecon: Life After Capitalism'' was published further outlining participatory economics in a more accessible, less academic format.{{r|lac1}} The book was translated into 20 languages.{{r|lac4}} Reviewing the book [[Paul Ormerod]] felt Albert's criticisms of [[capitalism]] were unfounded.{{r|lac5}} Albert spoke at the [[World Social Forum]] in the same year.{{r|lac2}} He spoke at [[European Social Forum]] in 2004.{{r|lac3}}

Albert was a founding member of the International Organization for a Participatory Society, in 2012.{{r|iops1|iops2}}

[[Sean Michael Wilson]] created a comic book based on Albert and his ideas in 2013.{{r|comic1|comic2}}

==Beliefs==
Albert identifies himself as a [[market abolitionist]] and believes markets should be replaced with [[participatory economics]].{{r|abo1|abo2|abo3|page3=222|page4=284|abo4}}

==Criticism==
In 2006, [[David Schweickart]] wrote a detailed critique of participatory economics called ''Nonsense on Stilts: Michael Albert's Parecon''. He claimed three fundamental features of the economic system are flawed.{{r|crit1}}
